CS 330 is a software-engineering course, not a cybersecurity course: nothing here asks you to scan, test or touch any system you do not own. What applies in full: the licence and copyright rules (section 4), fictional personal data only in anything you submit (sections 6.7, 18.2), the link-and-download checklist (section 14, Annex C), academic integrity (section 18) and the Cyber.SoHo Code of Ethics (section 9). No vendor, platform or institution named on this page is affiliated with Cyber.SoHo (section 5). The student acknowledgement (Annex A, e-signature) will be provided separately.

What you actually do, step by step

This page shows the lab as a sequence of short animations — one per step — so you can see the shape of the work before you start. The full instructions, the case cards and the template are in the lab document; this is the map. Every animation loops; the Pause button under each shows its last frame, which is also the frame worth keeping open while you work. The examples use a fictional team (Team Falcon) and the QueueLess product from the course menu; every name in them is invented.

All tools are open. Markdown, Git, GitHub, a drawing tool — every tool in these animations is a suggestion. Use any equivalent your team has, research it first (who makes it, what it costs, what it does with your data), or build your own. Only the file and the tag are fixed.

Before Step 1 — where your three hours go

Animated · loops · ~5 frames

The lecture hour is not lab work. The two hours in class are the break, one hundred minutes of Studio and the wrap-up. The hour at home finishes the file — it never starts new work. If you pass three hours, stop and write the professor a line about what is missing.

Step 1 · Set up

5 minutes · 1:10–1:15
Animated · loops · ~5 frames

Visual Studio Code ships a new version every month; its menus and file explorer may look different from this drawing. The steps do not change, and any editor that saves plain text is fine — the file, not the tool, is the deliverable.

  • Open Brick 1 and read the vision sentence aloud, once — everything you write today belongs to that product.
  • Copy the template to /docs/02-ethics-brief.md in the repository (not on one laptop). Fill the header: team, product, date, members, tools, AI declaration.
  • Name the Scribe. Start a timer everyone can see.
Done when: the file exists in the repository on the right path, with the header filled.

Step 2 · Case carousel

25 minutes · 1:15–1:40 · three stations × 8 minutes
Animated · loops · ~6 frames

The text of the Software Engineering Code of Ethics (version 5.2) has not changed since 1999; the web pages that host it are redesigned from time to time. If a link moves, search for “Software Engineering Code of Ethics” on computer.org or acm.org.

  • At each station: read the card together (2′), then write one sentence for each question, using the principle names of the Code.
  • Q1 — which principle(s) were broken, and by whom (engineer · manager · company · regulator)? Q2 — the moment one person could have changed the outcome: what would you have done, and what would it have cost you?
  • Leave the answer sheet on the table when the bell rings; the next station is one minute away.
Done when: six sentences exist — two per case — each naming at least one principle.

Step 3 · Debrief — the pattern

10 minutes · 1:40–1:50
Animated · loops · ~5 frames
  • The professor asks the room what the three cases have in common. Listen, argue, then write your team's one sentence under “What the three cases have in common” in section 1.
  • If you can name the pattern, you will recognise it when it starts happening to you.
Done when: the sentence is written — yours, not the room's.

Step 4 · Stakeholder map

15 minutes · 1:50–2:05
Animated · loops · ~6 frames

diagrams.net and Excalidraw update their interfaces often; a whiteboard photo never goes out of date. Any drawing you can read next week is acceptable.

  • Five groups, roles not names, three columns each: who · what they want from the product · what could hurt them.
  • Minimums: Users 2 · Client 1 · Operators 1 · Affected third parties 2 · Regulators and rules 2 — name the privacy law that applies where your product would run (GDPR, PIPEDA, FERPA) and the accessibility standard (WCAG 2.2).
  • Eight stakeholders is the target; more than twelve means you are listing, not thinking.
Done when: every group has its minimum and every stakeholder has the three columns filled.

Step 5 · Harms & mitigations table

20 minutes · 2:05–2:25
Animated · loops · ~6 frames
  • At least five rows. A harm is a concrete bad outcome for a named stakeholder; a mitigation is an action you can point at later — a requirement, a screen, a team rule. “We will not build that feature” counts.
  • Likelihood if you did nothing: Low (once a semester or less) · Medium (about monthly) · High (weekly or more).
  • One row must come from the third parties; one row must be about data (it feeds Step 6); every row names a principle.
Done when: five rows, every cell filled, a principle on every row.

Step 6 · Data & privacy note

10 minutes · 2:25–2:35
Animated · loops · ~5 frames
  • One line per piece of personal data the product would hold: what · why · how long · how the person consents and withdraws.
  • Two closing lines: who inside the team or the client can see it, and what you decided not to collect — and why.
  • Fictional examples only. No real classmate, customer or e-mail address, ever (Legal Notice, sections 6.7 and 18.2).
Done when: every data item has its four answers and the two closing lines exist.

Step 7 · Cross-team review

15 minutes · 2:35–2:50 · then the 10-minute wrap-up
Animated · loops · ~5 frames
  • Swap briefs with the team the professor pairs you with. Read theirs for five minutes.
  • Give two comments on the review sheet: one risk you missed and one mitigation that would not work, and why. Copy the two you receive into section 5 and answer each: Accept (what you change) or Decline (why). Declining is allowed; ignoring is not.
  • Wrap-up: exit ticket — “Which principle of the Code will your product test the most?” — then push your draft before you leave (git add · git commit · git push).
Done when: two comments given, two received and answered, the draft pushed.

At home · Steps 8–11

60 minutes, maximum · before Sunday, October 4, 23:59
Animated · loops · ~8 frames

Checked September 2026 with Git 2.55.0 (released June 29, 2026 — see git-scm.com). The commands shown have been stable for years. What changes often is the look of hosting sites: on GitHub the list of tags has moved between the branch switcher and a separate “Tags” page more than once. If the screen looks different from this drawing, search the page for the word Tags. Any Git host (GitLab, Codeberg, a server your team runs) works the same way. The LMS panel is a schematic. Your course LMS (Learning Management System) will look different — look for the Block 2 submission folder; the professor shows it in the wrap-up.

Step 8 · Clean the brief · 20′

Apply the comments you accepted. Replace every slogan with an action. Check the counts against the Definition of Done. Read the file once as a stranger would.

Step 9 · Reflection · 15′

Each member: 150 words, own name, The engineer I want to be — a principle you would hold to even at a cost; a moment in one case where you would have spoken; one habit you start this semester. Your own words. AI (Artificial Intelligence) tools only if declared in section 0 of the brief.

Step 10 · Ship it · 10′

git add docs/02-ethics-brief.md docs/img/
git commit -m "Block 2: stakeholder & ethics brief"
git tag block2
git push
git push origin block2

Confirm the tag is visible on the hosting site, then post the repository link and the tag name on the LMS. One submission per team.

Step 11 · Read and memorise · 15′

Pressman 9e, chapters 5 and 6; the Code once more; the nine flash-cards of the week. Then stop.

Definition of Done — tick before you submit

The boxes are for you; they save nothing.
